For Atheists, who is Jesus to you, given historical evidence of his existence? Which Jesus are we talking about? The Jesus of the Gospels, or the historical Jesus without all the myth and legend tacked on? By way of example, consider Saint Nicholas vs. Santa Claus. Santa Claus may be based on a real, historical Saint Nicholas, but the legend has diverged so far from reality in all that time, that the characters contain very little in common. What's more, we don't actually know all that much about the real Saint Nicholas, so it's tough to say too much about him. That's the same way it is for the historical Jesus vs. the Gospel Jesus. The historical Jesus probably existed, but there's just very little in the way of reliable evidence on what he might have been like. Paul's authentic letters are some of the earliest mentions we have of Jesus, but they don't contain much in the way of biographical details. The Gospels are much more detailed, but also come from decades later, and were almost certainly second hand accounts spread by word of mouth before educated Christians finally committed them to paper. Considering how quickly urban legends can pop up in the modern day, and how often we see misattributed quotes (Mark Twain didn't say nearly so much as the Internet memes claim he did), a decades long gap is a lot of time for the legends around Jesus to grow and morph. So it's really tough to say much of anything about the historical Jesus – whether he was an honest preacher whose image got embellished over the years, a conman who intentionally mislead people with lies and sleight of hand tricks to build a reputation as a miracle worker, a bit of a crazy religious zealot who might have believed a lot of what he said, or just about anything else you can imagine. We've got plenty of modern day religious figures as examples for any of those scenarios. As far as the more legendary Jesus of the Gospels, as I've said before, my opinion is a bit mixed. Everyone is plenty familiar with the good things he said (feed the poor, love your neighbor, don't judge others, etc.), so there's no need for me to repeat all that here. But he also had plenty of more troubling teachings. Since I've already written about this before (Jeff Lewis's answer to Being an atheist, I know you do not believe in God, but do you see Jesus (the character) as being a good role model? Why?), I'm going to quote that here: But let's not forget who the historical Jesus was – a religious extremist and a cult leader. He supposedly told his followers things like, "Whoever is not with me is against me," and "Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple." If a Jim Jones, David Koresh, or L. Ron Hubbard were to say such things we'd call them out as gigantic red flags. Just because Christianity went on to become a major religion doesn't mean it was okay when (if) Jesus said those things in the first place. Although Christians were quick to rationalize/accommodate Jesus's failed prophecies, he himself seemed to believe that the coming age of the Son of Man was imminent, "Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." That, and his belief that God would take care of people with enough faith, led to several teachings that are rather irresponsible if you actually have to plan for the future. "Therefore do not worry, saying, ‘What will we eat?’ or ‘What will we drink?’ or ‘What will we wear?’ For it is the Gentiles who strive for all these things; and indeed your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things." Or his admonition to the rich young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell your possessions, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me." At times, Jesus also had a bit of a black & white way of looking at the world that lacked subtlety or nuance. One that's bothered me for a while is the way he equated temptation to actually acting on it. Consider his teaching on lust, "But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart." Seriously, ask any married person if they'd be as upset at their spouse for a momentary feeling of lust, or actually committing adultery. This type of teaching just sets people up for failure. Instead of framing it as a positive that someone was able to overcome their temptations, it berates people for having normal, natural emotions in the first place. [Going even further, you could frame that as adultery being no worse than lust, so if you've already lusted after somebody, you're not doing anything worse by actually carrying trough with action.] Then there's the whole episode with the money changers in the temple, which very well may have been the incident that led to his crucifixion. Now, it's one thing to have strong principles and to stand up for them. But it's another thing altogether to go onto somebody else's property to cause a major disturbance, vandalize the premises, and assault the people there. I mean, I can think of one church in particular here in my own town that I don't like, but I'm not going to show up there on a Sunday morning, smash up their altar, and start chasing people out of the pews. That's not how mature, sensible people handle disagreements. Finally, this last one may be a little unfair to the historical Jesus, since it comes from one of the stories that arose after his death, but I've always hated the doubting Thomas story. "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe." No, no, no. It is not a virtue to believe things without evidence. It's this type of gullibility and naivety that leads people to give all their money to Nigerian princesses. Critical thinking and skepticism (not to be confused with cynicism) are skillsets that should be nurtured and celebrated, not discouraged. So, it's tough to say anything about the historical Jesus, because we just don't have much reliable evidence to know what he was really like. The Jesus of the Gospels was a mixed bag, with some good teachings, but plenty of troubling ones. Related:

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? It's not fiction in the same sense as a novel, where one person sat down to write a story. Much of what ended up in the Bible were legends and stories that had been floating around in that culture for generations, spread largely by word of mouth and oral history. Sure, every once in a while some scribe might have written down a particular version of one of the legends, but these wouldn't have initially taken on the authority of 'scripture', and the legends would continue to develop within the larger society. As a more modern day example, consider Grimm's Fairy Tales. The Brothers Grimm didn't invent these stories themselves. They went around collecting stories from German folklore. You can see this in the books now referred to as the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy). By using critical analysis to study these books, it's clear that they were the result of combining four prior traditions, now known as the Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, and Deuteronomist sources, with a round of editing by a person or group known as the Redactor. As just one example from the Old Testament, the Noah's Ark story can trace its origins back to older Sumerian flood myths such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis. And even the story within Genesis is an intertwining of the Priestly and Yahwist traditions, with conflicting details throughout the story, such as the number of animals to take aboard (one pair of each kind vs. seven pairs of the clean kinds), how long the flood lasted (40 days in the Yahwist source per Genesis 7:17 vs. 150 days in the Priestly source per Genesis 7:24), and twice repeating that Noah went into the ark (7:7-9 and again at 7:13-16). The New Testament development was a bit more rapid, but it was still the result of stories being passed along by word of mouth for decades before a few educated converts to Christianity decided to write them down. Some of those accounts eventually acquired enough of a reputation to be included in the official canon, but many more never acquired the status of 'scriptures', and are regarded as merely early Christian writing. Basically, it's the same as many other mythologies. Nobody necessarily sits down with the intent to create a story from scratch. It's stories that get passed on orally from generation to generation, that develop and morph over the years. Some scribes write down the stories from time to time, and the written versions that strike a chord become canonical.

Why aren't autogyros as popular as cars? I'm not sure everyone knows exactly what an autogyro is, so let me start off with some background. Way back in the day, before practical helicopters, autogyros were the first practical rotorcraft. But unlike helicopters, the rotor isn't powered in flight. It's made to spin by aerodynamic means, technically known as autorotation. So, autogyros can't hover, and they still need a propeller or some other form of propulsion. Still, back in those early days, autogyros gave much better short field performance than airplanes, along with improved low speed handling characteristics (no stall since your ‘wings’ are rotating independently of your airspeed). As autogyro technology advanced, they even developed jump takeoff abilities, where a clutched driveshaft from the engine would spin up the rotor to a high rpm on the ground, and then increase the pitch on the blades and use that rotor inertia to jump into the air. The rotor head can still be simpler than a helicopter, and you also don’t need a tail rotor (no torque to the rotor once you’re in the air). Here’s a Pitcairn PA-36, towards the zenith of autogyro popularity before being eclipsed by helicopters, demonstrating jump takeoff and short landing capabilities: Nowadays, gyros are mostly relegated to small recreational aircraft, not quite as mechanically complex as that PA-36 up above. They split the difference between airplanes and helicopters, while remaining much less complex and less expensive than helicopters. I’ve seen ultralight gyros take off in the space of about 25 ft, and touch down vertically with no roll out. ABOVE: A typical modern recreational autogyro SOURCE: AutoGyro MT-03 - Wikipedia Anyway, on to the question of why autogyros aren't as popular as cars. First, personal aircraft in general, from airplanes to helicopters to autogyros, are never going to be as popular as cars. The training to become a pilot is more extensive and regulated than earning a driver's license. The extra rigor of aircraft certification and maintenance drives higher prices. Aircraft, even rotorcraft, can only fly between locations that can easily accommodate aircraft (i.e. no door to door from your house to the mall). And bad weather and high winds are a much bigger deal for air travel, and would ground the aircraft during storms or fog that are a mere nuisance in cars. In other words, you'll still need cars, so personal aircraft would be your second or third vehicle. As far as why autogyros are even less popular than airplanes and helicopters, it's because they fall somewhere in the middle performance-wise, so they don't perform typical rotorcraft missions as well as helicopters, or fixed-wing missions as well as airplanes. If you need to hover, you need a helicopter. And if you want to fly fast, airplanes are more efficient than most gyros. There are some companies trying to push modern day gyros if you only need short/zero roll takeoffs and landings but not full hover capability, but truth be told, the market hasn’t really embraced gyros very widely beyond personal / recreational vehicles. As an aside, there have been efforts over the years for even more advanced autogyros. Particularly well known (at least among aviation nerds) was the Fairey Rotodyne. They actually powered the rotor with tip jets for takeoff and landing, so it could hover. But then they transitioned the rotor to autorotation in flight, reducing the rpm to reduce drag and using the wings and props to fly more like an airplane. It's major drawback was that those tip jets were LOUD, though perhaps that might have been addressed had it not been for politics when Fairey was acquired by Westland Aircraft who already had a competing rotorcraft division. Anyway, it was still an interesting concept:

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? In any sufficiently large group, you can always find a few cranks and screwballs with odd conspiracy theories. In the U.S., there are something like 600,000 people with pilot licenses, with around 100,000 of those working in commercial aviation (How Many Pilots Are In The US?), not to mention military pilots. If even just one out of a thousand of those pilots believe in a flat earth, that's 600 total pilots, or 100 commercial pilots – certainly enough to throw together in a YouTube video with a long list of 'testimonials'. Now, I'm pretty immersed in aviation myself. My own job is an aerospace engineer. I got my pilot's license back when I was in college, working a couple summers at the airport. I currently live in a town with a lot of influence from our local Air Force base. So, between my job and personal life, I know lots of pilots, aerospace engineers, and even a few air traffic controllers. And I don't personally know any of them who believe in a flat earth. It's the type of thing we joke about from time to time, but not something that anybody takes seriously. I don't know of any polls or studies to put numbers to this, but if you want some perspectives beyond my own, you can check out pages like this reddit thread: Or read this article from AOPA about a pilot's experience flying around the world: In short, there are so many pilots that I'm sure you can find a handful who think the Earth is flat. But these guys certainly aren't representative of the field as a whole.

Why do scientist always discount the creation theory, as opposed to the evolutionary theory? Well, they didn't always discount creationism. Back in the early 1800s, creationism really was the dominant paradigm in biology. It's pinnacle was perhaps William Paley's famous book from 1802, Natural Theology, which included his famous Watchmaker analogy. Darwin himself summarized the debate in the introduction to the 6th edition of On the Origin of Species (emphasis mine): I will here give a brief sketch of the progress of opinion on the Origin of Species. Until recently the great majority of naturalists believed that species were immutable productions, and had been separately created. This view has been ably maintained by many authors. Some few naturalists, on the other hand, have believed that species undergo modification, and that the existing forms of life are the descendants by true generation of pre existing forms. In his autobiography, Darwin wrote a brief passage about how even he had been convinced by Paley's creationist arguments prior to discovering natural selection (emphasis mine, again): The old argument of design in nature, as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered. We can no longer argue that, for instance, the beautiful hinge of a bivalve shell must have been made by an intelligent being, like the hinge of a door by man. There seems to be no more design in the variability of organic beings and in the action of natural selection, than in the course which the wind blows. Everything in nature is the result of fixed laws. If you want to see how much of The Origin was devoted to countering creationism, just open up a copy on your computer and do a search for 'creat', which will highlight all the incidences of creation, creationism, creator, etc. I did it myself and counted something like 128 mentions of creationism or related terms (make sure you avoid 'false positives' like creature). That's a whole lot of discussion of creationism. This answer is already hinting at why creationism is no longer taken seriously – it was replaced by a better theory that's a much better match to the evidence. And in the 150 years since Darwin published The Origin, that evidence has only gotten stronger. It’s very similar to why chemists no longer debate oxidation vs. phlogiston theory. Or to put it another way, this is a debate that was settled over a century ago, so scientists have moved on to more interesting questions.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus? Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? In many cases, there isn't a single main ingredient. All of the ingredients are important and work together in harmony. Take perhaps my favorite sandwich (and it's a fierce competition, since so many sandwiches are so damn good), the BLT. IMAGE SOURCE: BLT (Bacon, Lettuce and Tomato Sandwich) It's only five ingredients – the bacon, lettuce, and tomato that the name implies, plus toast and mayo. Screw up any single one of those ingredients, and your sandwich is hosed. And believe me, I've had hosed BLTs where restaurants tried to 'dress it up', only to ruin the balance. Things like using ciabatta instead of sliced bread, piling what seems like an entire pound of bacon onto a single sandwich, or using some trendy lettuce instead of a nice, crispy iceberg lettuce. You've got to get all of the ingredients right, and in the right balance, or the sandwich just isn't the same. Even something like a hoagie, which may seem like just piling ingredient on top of ingredient, still relies on getting all of the individual ingredients right. I once wrote an answer explaining how Subway sandwiches are only mediocre in comparison to real hoagies (Jeff Lewis's answer to Why don't people like Subway subs?), and posted this image for the comparison: Just at a glance, you can see the difference between the sterile excuse for a sandwich in the top left compared to the other three proper hoagies. And it’s not just one thing that makes the difference. Good hoagies need to get every single ingredient right, from the bread to the meats to the cheese to properly shaved onions. All of the ingredients are important. Good sandwiches don't have a single main ingredient. Every ingredient works together to make a sandwich what it is.

Isn't it crazy that 1 man managed to convince billions of people that they evolved from an animal? Actually, yes it is. That's why Darwin is held in such high esteem as the genius he was, and why he was granted the honor of being buried in Westminster Abbey. Other naturalists had proposed ideas of transubstantiation before Charles Darwin, including his grandfather Erasmus Darwin. However, none of those predecessors had managed to convince the larger scientific establishment to take evolution particularly seriously. And Edward Blyth had hit on ideas of natural selection before Darwin published the Origin, though Blyth's comments on the matter went largely unnoticed. Somewhat famously (at least among us nerds), William Wallace also discovered natural selection independently, and even submitted a joint presentation of papers with Darwin to the Linnaean Society of London in 1858. But this submission also didn't have much impact. What did have tremendous impact was when Darwin finally published his book, On the Origin of Species, in 1859. The arguments and evidence he compiled in that book were enormously compelling. Practically overnight, evolution and universal common descent went from a somewhat disreputable position among fringe academics to accepted mainstream science. It was a monumental work on par with the likes of Newton and Einstein. Much of science progresses by incremental contributions from many different researchers. The subsequent history of evolutionary science after Darwin does follow this more general pattern. Looking through the Wikipedia article on the Modern synthesis, you find plenty of contributors like Ernst Mayr, G. Ledyard Stebbins, Theodosius Dobzhansky, E. B. Ford, Bernhard Rensch, Ivan Schmalhausen, George Gaylord Simpson, R. A. Fisher, William Bateson, Julian Huxley, J.B.S. Haldane, and more. But none of those folks, as intelligent as they were, had the same paradigm shifting impact as Charles Darwin. To put it another way, human knowledge had finally progressed to the point where discovering evolution was practically inevitable. It would have happened eventually. But without Darwin, it would have been a more prolonged process that would have taken a bit longer, and the folks who contributed would probably still be mentioned in the history books, but they wouldn't be household names (just look to Alfred Wegener and continental drift). Darwin was a true genius, with a monumental impact on biology. So yes, it is always a bit crazy when you come across such singular geniuses.

If a Starship without any payload can barely reach up to orbital speeds while expending almost ALL of the fuel within it, then could it be that SpaceX underestimated how easy/difficulty would be conceiving a fully reusable craft? Look, I've got my reservations about SpaceX's approach to safety with their 'Let's just blow stuff up till it quits blowing up approach'*, and I think that they can sometimes be a bit overhyped by Musk fanbois.** But let's keep things in perspective. They're a company with tons of talent from professional aerospace engineers. Even if they underestimated the difficulty of this approach back in the very beginning, by the time you're building and testing full scale prototypes, you've already gone through feasibility studies, trade studies, preliminary design, detail design, and tons and tons of analysis. The vehicle is performing more or less as predicted, and has the potential to be a truly awesome rocket once all the bugs are worked out. Look to Frank Norris's answer or Steve Baker's answer for more details, but the bottom line is that this vehicle will likely achieve its goal of delivering 100 – 150 tons of payload to orbit in the reusable configuration. That is quite an achievement. *My reservations with their 'Go-fast-fail-fast' approach is in the mindset, that if something hasn't gone wrong yet, then it must be good. That's way too reminiscent of the mindset that led to the Challenger disaster. Coming from an aviation background, myself, the standard level of safety for airliners is a probability of catastrophic failure of less than 1 per billion flight hours. You can't demonstrate that with a mere 100 flights with only around 10 minutes each getting to orbit and another 20 minutes for re-entry and landing. You either need prohibitive numbers of test flights, or you need to do lots and lots of traditional analysis. But if it takes half a dozen attempts to get even your first successful full flight, then your traditional analysis couldn't have been all that robust. On the other hand, other rocket manufacturers have plenty of failures, as well, so extreme risk in comparison to aviation just seems to be part of the game (though when Musk starts his dreaming about sending millions of people to Mars, that's when this safety approach becomes irresponsible). **In fairness, while Musk fanbois might overhype SpaceX, there are plenty of folks who go too far the other way, criticizing SpaceX too harshly merely because Musk himself seems to be a bit of a jackass. Whatever you think of Musk shouldn't detract from the real accomplishments of SpaceX. And remember, the company has many, many more engineers and technicians working there to achieve their successes.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? The short answer is not much. The long answer is complicated, depending on exactly what you mean by bicycles and how much freedom you'll allow in interpreting the question. The first thing to note, that many people don't seem to realize, is that pedaling to power a generator gets harder and harder the more electrical power you have to provide. They just see the wires, and seem to think that it's no harder than pedaling a free-wheeling bike. But once you try to actually create current with those wires, they create magnetic fields. And those magnetic fields make it more difficult to turn the generator. The more power, the stronger the magnetic field, and the harder it is to pedal. It all goes back to the conservation of energy, and the fact that you can't get something for nothing. Moving on, if you mean stationary cycles, where instead of moving, you're just driving a generator, then you're not going to get much energy at all. Loring Chien already went through the math in his answer. Even taking it to the extreme of people riding such machines for 12 hours a day every day, you only get 10% of the world's electric consumption (the average person can only maintain around 50 - 100 W continuously). And of course, that extreme scenario is not at all practical. You can't do your real job when riding a stationary bike. So if you cut people’s time down to a somewhat more realistic 1 hr per day to leave them time to do other things, then you’re looking at less than 1% of the world’s electric consumption. But even that’s over-estimating the net results. If people are going to perform that much physical exercise daily, their calorie requirements are going to go up. That means more food needs to be grown, stored, and transported, and all of that takes energy. How much of that energy comes from electricity vs. petroleum based fuel is dependent on how quickly EVs displace IC engines, but it’s certainly going to be something (and non-negligible when you’re talking about changes to diet on the scale of the entire world’s population). If you meant adding a generator to regular bikes that generated electricity during the course of normal riding, the numbers come out even lower. Recalling that you can’t get something for nothing, a generator that’s driven through a direct mechanical connection is going to feel like riding the brakes, with the braking force being higher the more power you try to generate. Alternatively, a wind powered generator is going to increase your drag, again forcing you to have to pedal harder. Basically, since you need power to propel the bike, you have to settle for only a fraction of the power that the person can generate going to the generator. That’s why existing generators on bikes are only used for very lower power applications like lights. In short, you’ll generate well, well short of even the 1% from the previous scenario. What about the power savings if everybody rode bikes instead of driving in cars? Now, you’re looking at a double impact, because bikes are much smaller than cars and so don’t require as much power. i.e. The benefit is not just in using human power, but in not needing as much power to begin with. Of course, if you’re just looking at electricity, this is going to be a bigger effect as EVs become more common. What makes this complicated to analyze is that cycling can only replace some uses of automobiles, not all of them, so you have to take that into account. Here’s one study, Ditching the car for walking or biking just one day a week cuts carbon footprint,. If we take CO2 as a proxy for energy consumption, that study found “If just 10% of the population were to change travel behaviour, the emissions savings would be around 4% of lifecycle CO2 emissions from all car travel.” Based on a couple other sources (the Energy Information Administration and the Bureau of Tranpsportation Statistics), transportation in total makes up 37% of U.S. energy consumption, while light-duty short wheelbase vehicles (i.e. cars) makes up 40.3% of that, or around 15% of the total energy consumption. So a 4% savings on automobiles is around a half percent total energy savings. But if you upped that “10% of the population” to “100% of the population”, and it scaled linearly to a 40% savings on car travel, you’d end up with a 6% savings in total energy consumption. That’s not exactly huge, but it’s not negligible, either. To sum up, none of the scenarios result in huge energy savings. Loring Chien’s calculation of people riding all day, every day, still only results in 10% of the world’s electricity requirements. Reducing people’s time on the bikes to 1 hr a day drops that to less than 1%. Putting generators on existing bikes for transportation generates an even smaller percentage than that. The most realistic and achievable scenario is to get people to ride their bikes instead of driving their cars for trips where it’s feasible. Depending on how many people you can get to do this, you’re looking at around 0.5% total energy savings in a more feasible scenario, or 6% in an overly optimistic scenario. But a few percent here and a few percent there can eventually add up to significant savings.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? You've got a weird way of approaching this question. Take fairies, for example. As you said, if you "can't make [your]self believe something without evidence", and there's no compelling evidence for the existence of fairies, the default position is to lack belief in fairies, or to take a non-fairiest worldview. If you needed some type of positive evidence for the non-existence of fairies, you'd be stuck in some weird ontological limbo. With no evidence for the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in fairies, but with no evidence against the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in their non-existence. But it's not just fairies. This goes for anything. You can build up positive evidence for the existence of something. It's much, much harder to build up evidence for the non-existence of something. That's why the burden of proof has developed the way it has. In general, it's up to the person claiming that something exists to prove their case. The rest of us have no need to take their claims seriously until they have such evidence. To borrow a somewhat silly example from the Internet, do you have any evidence against the existence of Eric The God-Eating Magic Penguin? Wouldn't it seem a bit ridiculous to say that just because you can't find any evidence against Eric, that you're not going to take the non-Ericist position? I hope you see where this is going. If gods exist, the burden of proof is on the people claiming that they exist. Until they can provide compelling evidence, the rest of us are under no obligation to take their claims seriously. Just like with fairies, the lack of evidence makes the default position a non-theistic worldview.

How does knob and tube wiring differ from modern wiring systems? All AC house wiring has at least a hot line and a neutral line. The hot line carries high voltage and the power to run your appliances. The neutral line will be at essentially zero voltage relative to ground, and provides the return path to close the circuit. In knob and tube wiring, the hot line and the neutral line are carried in physically separated wires. These wires are ideally covered in insulation, and then further isolated from the framing of your house with the namesake non-conducting ceramic knobs and tubes. Though I say 'ideally' covered in insulation, because with the age of many knob and tube installations, the insulation may have degraded. ABOVE: The basics of knob and tube wiring SOURCE: Knob and Tube Wiring To branch out from the main runs in knob and tube wiring, the wires need to be spliced. The insulation will have been stripped away from a section of the wire, and then the spliced wire will be wrapped around it and soldered to make a good connection, before being covered up again with insulating tape. Here's what a good splice looks like from the outside: SOURCE: Knob & Tube Electrical Wiring FAQs And here's a diagram of what it typically looks like underneath the tape: SOURCE: electrical splices guide for residential electrical wiring and circuits Modern wiring typically uses a type of wire commonly referred to by the trade name of Romex (or more generically as non-metallic sheathed cable). The typical configuration is to have the hot line, a neutral line, and a ground line all within the same cable, with the hot line and neutral line being encased in their own insulation. The ground line won't carry any current under normal circumstances, but it provides an alternative path to ground as an additional safety feature. It usually ends up being connected to things like metal chassis/cases of appliances, so that if there was a short circuit to the case, the ground wire would carry that electricity rather than somebody touching the appliance. It's also possible to get Romex with even more conductors in a single cable, such as for appliances running at 240 V that need to the two hot wires at different phases, or for things like 2-way light switches, where the wires act as 'travelers', and may or may not be hot depending on the position of the switches. And there’s also metallic clad armored cable for when you need more protection than the PVC sheathing from Romex. SOURCE: Types of Wires & Cables ABOVE: Example of a traveler wire SOURCE: What Is a Traveler Wire and Why Is It Important? Modern wiring also does all connections in junction boxes, rather that at unmarked splices. In a few cases, this might be a pure junction box that does nothing but connect wires. But more often than not, the junction box is at an electrical outlet or switch, which lets you daisy chain outlets on a single circuit. ABOVE: Feed through vs. pigtail connections SOURCE: https://www.jlconline.com/how-to/electrical/q-a-to-pigtail-or-not-to-pigtail_o ABOVE: Typical wiring for multiple outlets SOURCE: https://www.reddit.com/r/ElectricianU/comments/m40m6a/wiring_outlets_in_seriesparallel/ Anyway, those are the basics. The general principles of electricity are obviously still the same. But there are a lot of differences in the details of how each system gets implemented, all based on lessons learned over the years to make modern wiring easier and safer.

Is a ruler exactly 12 inches? Surely if you zoom in trillions and trillions and trillions of times, then the length of the ruler has to be ever so slightly different than exactly 12 inches, correct? This brings up a topic that I found enormously fascinating when I first became an engineer, and that I think is drastically underappreciated by the general public – tolerances. This is such a huge topic that I could write an entire book about it, because people have, in fact, written entire books about it. ABOVE: 367 pages worth of explanation about tolerancing SOURCE: Amazon The issue, like you've correctly surmised, is that it's essentially impossible to make an object exactly a certain dimension. And in truth, you don't usually need it to be that exact, anyway. So, when I make a technical drawing to send to a machine shop to get a part made, I don't just call out the dimensions of all the features. I also call out how close the actual measurements of the finished part need to be to those dimensions on the drawing. A typical title block on a drawing might look something like this, with standard tolerances based on how many decimal points you use in a dimension: So, if I call out a length as 3.0, that gets a tolerance of ±0.03", so the machine shop could make that feature anything from 2.97" to 3.03", and it would be acceptable. If it was something that needed to be very precise, then I might call out the dimension as 3.0000, in which case the machine shop would have to make the feature to within ±0.001", or 2.999" to 3.001". Sometimes, those default tolerances aren't enough. It might be something like a hole that would work out okay if it was a little too big, but not too small, so you might specify an asymmetrical tolerance, like +.01/-0. Or, it might be something like a bearing housing that needs to be even tighter than 0.001". In those cases, you'll specify the tolerance right at the dimension on the drawing, rather than rely on the default dimensions from the title block. There are all types of things that can be covered in tolerancing – lengths, circularity, flatness, concentricity, perpendicularity, etc. We don't always take the time to mark such figures like we should, sometimes relying on implied understandings and quality workmanship, but that can also get you into trouble. I remember one specialized nut we designed that had to fit inside another hole without a whole lot of clearance. The nut was threaded on the inside and round on the outside, with a couple flats carved on the top to fit a wrench. We just assumed that the part would get made on a lathe and that the features would all be concentric, so we didn't think to specify a concentricity tolerance. Well, however the machine shop made it, the center bore of the nut with the threads wasn't concentric with the outer diameter, so it didn't fit into that hole it needed to fit into. But since we didn't specify a concentricity tolerance, we had no grounds to reject the part. We just had to eat the cost, redo the drawing, and pay them to make another one. Measuring parts is another whole artform unto itself. We have instruments that are capable of high precision measurements, such as micrometers, dial calipers, and even (shudder) Vernier calipers. But when you're measuring things on the order of a few thousandths of an inch, it doesn't take too much force on the instrument to deform the part or the instrument itself to give a false reading. I'm somewhat handy at getting reasonable measurements with my dial caliper, but I always left the real measurements to the machinists and QA inspectors – I trusted them a whole lot more. ABOVE: A dial caliper with .001" graduations – it would be easy to push too hard and get that to read 0.712″ instead of the 0.710″ it currently shows SOURCE: https://instrumentation.com/120a-6-dial-caliper-hardened-stainless-steel-0-6-range-001-graduations.aspx Getting back to your original question, the tolerance on a typical 12" ruler that you'd buy from Walmart usually won't be just super tight. The smallest divisions on the ruler are liable to only be 1/16" of inch to begin with, or 0.0625". If that's the smallest mark on the ruler, nobody's going to notice if it's off by a few thousandths of an inch. So the tolerance for making such rulers can be a bit on the loose side. I didn't even get into Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, which is another entire topic. It expands on the basic level of tolerancing I already described in this answer. It's a bit more complicated than traditional tolerancing, but ideally gives more wiggle room to the manufacturers by understanding the intent behind the tolerances.

What makes Google Maps superior to Apple Maps? One reason – north up maps. Maybe I'm just old fashioned from the old days of using paper maps*. But I really, really, really prefer maps to always be oriented as north up when I'm driving. I know it might not be the most intuitive when you need to make split second decisions. But in the long run, it gives you a much better perspective and sense of orientation. Especially when you're in an area where you might be spending some time and not just driving through once, it really helps you learn the area. I have a sense of the actual cardinal direction I'm heading, not just 'straight ahead'. I can see where neighborhoods lie in relation to each other. I can build up a mental map that corresponds to the map I see on the screen. In contrast, the maps that are constantly rotating to align with your direction of travel just completely destroy that sense of awareness and perspective. When I spent a few months in El Paso a couple years ago, I learned my way around much quicker thanks to Google Maps always keeping the map with north up. Otherwise, despite an ignominious beginning**, Apple Maps has grown into a decent app. It even seems to do better than Google Maps at some things, like telling you which lane to be in, and giving you more than one next step at a time. But until Apple decides to put in an option for users to keep the map oriented as north up even in guidance mode, I'm simply not going to use it. *I remember back when I was a kid, on road trip vacations, or when we first moved from Pennsylvania to Maryland, and I'd sit in the back seat of the car following along on a map to see where we were. Maybe it was all those years of practice that helps me follow along on north up maps, when so many other folks I know seem to get confused by it. **If you look at the other answers to this question, the ones trashing Apple Maps tend to be several years old. It really is a decent app, now, minus that one, monumental shortcoming.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? First off, this question hits one of my pet peeves – using the word 'necessary' without any context, implying that 'necessary' is some intrinsic property all on its own. It isn't. Just about every time this word is used, it's in relation to a specific outcome. For example, are fermentable sugar and yeast necessary ingredients? Yes if you're making beer or bread. Not so much if you're grilling a steak. Considering that TV itself isn't a necessity, hardly anything around the medium is necessary in any universal sense. It all depends on what outcomes you want. So, if you're asking if these disclaimers are necessary – necessary for what? If you wanted to be cynical, you could say that the purpose of these disclaimers is merely a way to silence the busybodies with a token message that only lasts a few seconds, that most viewers will forget about almost as soon as the action starts. The network can still show controversial or 'problematic' content essentially unaltered, retaining most of the audience that enjoys those shows (and their associated advertising dollars). The networks have balanced the conflicting influences of alienating more politically correct viewers to losing more old fashioned viewers, and figured these disclaimers were the best compromise. It's the free market at work. If you want to be more charitable about their motivations, such disclaimers do play at least a small part in consciousness raising. It may only be a short message, but at least it's putting it in people's heads that these depictions may not be so benign. And so when they do watch these shows, they're not just uncritically accepting such depictions as right or normal. I think this is especially true when it comes to kids watching TV. I know, some folks like to say that parents should be aware of all the media their children are consuming. That's a bit unrealistic, not to mention a bit questionable advice in its own right. Such constant supervision has taken on its own derogatory term these days – helicopter parenting. On the other extreme, you have folks fondly remembering the 'good old days', when kids roamed their neighborhoods unsupervised for hours on end (and believe me, even back then, we found parents' stashes of 'questionable' media hidden in boxes in the attic). Ideal parenting is somewhere in between – a balance of oversight and child independence, where parents have a general idea of what their kids are up to, but not necessarily screening each and every TV show their kids are going to watch. And in this context, such disclaimers are important in the consciousness raising of children, who don't have the background and experience to fully understand such shows like adults. So yes. I think these disclaimers serve a purpose. They help in the consciousness raising of both nostalgic older viewers and younger first time viewers. And considering that it's such a short message and that the shows themselves are unaltered, it seems that it's only the most easily offended who get worked up about these disclaimers, anyway.

Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today? What you're referring to is saltationism (from the Latin term for jump), sometimes referred to a little more colorfully as the hopeful monster hypothesis. The idea was that large macromutations create new species in a single blow. But, as the colorful name and your question point out, how would such hopeful monsters find partners to mate with? This idea did have some proponents back in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but the incorporation of genetics into evolutionary theory and the Modern Synthesis caused the idea to be mostly abandoned, at least for sexually reproducing animals. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. Populations already have genetic diversity. It's why no two individuals look exactly alike. And genetic mutation is decently common. In us humans, for example, it seems that pretty much everybody has a handful of new mutations*. But this genetic diversity doesn't keep us (or other populations of animals) from mating. And the new mutations that do creep into the population don't instantly create new species. They just add to the existing genetic diversity. For a population to split into two species takes time and isolation. The population somehow gets split into two separate populations, let's say Population A and Population B, that can't or don't mate with each other. These constant mutations will continue to spontaneously arise in each population, but they'll be limited to their respective populations. Mutations that arise in Population A, for example, can mix into that population over generations as all those animals mate with each other, but as long as Population B remains isolated from Population A, those mutations won't jump over to Population B. They'll be limited to Population A. And the same goes vice versa for new mutations that arise in Population B. Over time, as each of these population acquires more and more different mutations, they'll become more and more distinct from each other. Eventually, they'll have become different enough to be new species, but it's still a gradual process, with no stark dividing line. ABOVE SOURCE: Islands of speciation and speciation on islands This also explains why species is such a fuzzy boundary, with 'lumpers' and 'splitters' often disagreeing on whether different populations should be separate species, or merely subspecies. For example, a single study from 2020 , showed that there could be anywhere from 2 to 6 different species of giraffe depending on which specific criteria you used to define species. But sexually reproducing animals aren't the only organisms out there. Many types of animals are hermaphrodites, with male and female reproductive organs on the same individual. Many plants also produce male and female reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) on the same plant. If one of these types of organisms were to experience a substantial mutation, then it could potentially create a new species with that individual. In fact, this actually has been observed decently often for plants (take a look at section 5.1 of this page, Observed Instances of Speciation). Another exception is animals that reproduce by parthenogenesis, which is just a fancy term to describe animals where an egg can develop without being fertilized by a male. A notable recent case is the marbled crayfish. Their ancestral species is the slough crayfish from Georgia and Florida. People captured slough crayfish for pets, which led to captive breeding to supply the pet trade. Some time around the mid '90s, somebody in Germany discovered the new species, marbled crayfish, which can reproduce parthenogenetically. This new species like arose from a mutation in a single individual. (You might also see these animals referred to by their German name, marmokrebs.) So, your intuition was partially right about sexually reproducing animals. Even if there were massive mutations that would create a new species in a single individual, the odds of such mutations happening simultaneously to create a male and female of that new species are so astronomically low as to be effectively impossible. But, that’s not the way speciation actually occurs in sexually reproducing animals. It’s a gradual process among populations due the accumulation of many, many mutations. But among other types of organisms that can reproduce by themselves and so don’t have the problem of being hopeful monsters, then speciation can sometimes happen in a single individual. * The overall mutation rate is on the order of 100 - 200 mutations per person. But given that something like 90% of our genome is junk DNA, most of those mutations don't do much at all. Still, it seems that we do all get at least a handful of mutations to functional DNA. WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? I think you might want to consider what travel was like just a century ago before calling the present state a nightmare. I wrote an answer once about travel in the 1800s and early 1900s (Jeff Lewis's answer to Before the industrial revolution when there were no cars or planes how did people travel and how far would they typically go?). A 30 mile trip would have been an all day affair back then. Now I can do that in around half an hour. It took Wilbur Wright a week to travel from Dayton, Ohio to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Google tells me I could make that drive in a little over 10 hrs, which is within reason for a single long day. Automobiles and the Interstate Highway System (or equivalent freeways in other countries) make relatively high speed long distance travel accessible to common people. As far as common sci-fi tropes like flying cars and holographic movies, you can't invent something physically impossible. As far as we know, there's no way to create levitating vehicles, except by already understood physics like magnets, which limits your altitude to something like a maglev train, or aerodynamics, which is basically just an aircraft, and we already have those. You're never going to see something like the cars in Blade Runner that just seem to float in midair with no visibile means of propulsion. Of course, there's more than one use of the term, flying car. If you mean an aircraft with folding wings or a folding rotor, people have already built prototypes of those. The big issue is that the compromises make them subpar aircraft and subpar ground transportation – the worst of both worlds. If you mean a dedicated aircraft that doesn't drive on the road, the issue comes down to physics and hover efficiency. Helicopters look the way they do for a reason. And even the new batch of eVTOL aircraft still have a large amount of total area for their lifting devices to have any type of reasonable efficiency. ABOVE: Various eVTOL Concepts – I don't think this is what most people think of when they hear the term 'flying car'. SOURCE: eVTOL is Almost Here: What About Pilot Training? The way holograms are portrayed in movies is somewhere between very, very difficult to impossible. Keep in mind that what we see is light heading towards our eyes coming from specific locations in space. You can't just make light originate from points in space from nothing. You need something to reflect it off of, or some medium that you can make glow at certain points to generate that light. Here's one of the approaches I've seen that comes closest to what people think of as sci-fi holograms, but just imagine the engineering difficulty of scaling this up to something that could generate an entire full color screen, without the particles interfering with each other, and with opacity (instead of just see through 'wireframes'). And other than the gee whiz factor, how useful would it even be? We've already got the ability to make 3D movies, and they only come and go as brief fads. People seem perfectly content with regular movies. And movie makers use that medium to frame shots and show things from specific perspectives. Horror movies would lose their jumps scares if you had a holographic representation of the entire scene and could see the monster hiding behind the bushes. So yeah, within our lifetimes, we probably are limited to only incremental improvements beyond our current technology. But our current technology is anything but a nightmare. It really is pretty amazing when you stop and think about it, and would have seemed like a technological marvel to people from just a century ago.

Why do so many people hate the self checkouts? Actually, I tend to prefer it. But it really depends on the implementation, and what the store was like before they brought in the self checkouts. Let me take my local Walmart as an example. Back in the days before self checkouts, they never had enough cashiers for the number of customers. There was no such thing as a quick trip to Walmart, because you inevitably got stuck in a long line waiting to check out. Then, when they did bring in self checkouts, they brought in dozens of them. So now, there's almost always at least one self-checkout open. And even if there is a line, it's more like a bank line, where everybody waits in one line, and then just goes to the next open checkout. So it doesn't matter if there are a few folks with full carts, because they're only tying up that one particular checkout, not the entire line. Now it really is possible to be in and out of Walmart in 5 minutes if I only need one thing. I've been to other stores, though, where they've only installed a limited number of self checkouts. And the worst offenders don't even go with the bank-style lines, but have separate lines for each self checkout. Those are annoying, where you may end up waiting longer than the pre-self-checkout days. My favorite modern checkout is Sam's Club (I'd imagine the other warehouse stores have this as well, but Wichita Falls, TX doesn't give you many options). You just download an app to your phone to scan the items as you shop, swipe a button to pay with a credit card on file, and then just briefly show your phone to the receipt checker on your way out the door. It's hard to get much quicker and convenient than that. But my second favorite checkout is at a small grocery chain called United Market Street, which has a good compromise between self checkouts and old school people. They do employ plenty of real life cashiers to scan your groceries, so the lines are rarely very long. And they even still have baggers, who take your groceries out to your car for you. They also have about half a dozen self checkouts, largely to replace the express checkout. So even the express line folks don't get all that inconvenienced by somebody cheating with a cart full of 50 things. Of course, you pay for it. Their prices aren't horrible, but they're definitely higher than Walmart or Aldi. As far as a few other answers I've seen about taking away low skill jobs, meh. The recent trend of online shopping seems to have taken care of that, with employees running around to fill all those online orders. My daughter did that for a bit at the aforementioned Market Street, and I see plenty of folks with that job at my local Walmart. So, until robots take over that, those jobs offset the loss of cashiers. So as long as it's done right, and considering that stores were skimping on cashiers even before self-checkouts were a thing, I've found self-checkouts to make shopping more convenient.

Back when I was still a Christian, I took that very seriously, and never would have dreamt of saying 'Oh my God' or 'Jesus Christ' as mere explitives. I mean, I knew there were much more serious issues that that commandment was referring to (What Does It Really Mean to Take the Lord’s Name in Vain?), but invoking the name of God just for emphasis on worldly concerns still fell under the rules. It's only now that I'm an atheist that I can say those expressions without fear of eternal damnation. So I sometimes do. Not because there's any mystical power about those terms in particular, but because taboo phrases carry more emotional impact than non-taboo phrases. Likewise, if I exclaim 'holy sh*t' or 'what the f*ck', I'm not literally referring to excrement or sexual intercourse. It's that those phrases carry so much emotional weight. Archeologists excavated a fossilised dinosaur, whole, and even found flesh/blood for DNA. Plus carbon-dating, it was proved dinosaurs died SIX MILLION years ago? However, Bible indicates it's been 5776 years now since Adam/Abraham. WHO IS LYING HERE? I'm going to focus on just carbon dating. There are already over 100 other answers to this question covering most everything else, but after skimming several dozen, most just say that carbon dating is only good to about 50k years without giving much of an explanation why. So let me give it a shot. The basis of carbon dating is that there are different isotopes of carbon in the atmosphere. By far the major one is carbon-12 (C12), so named because it has 6 protons and 6 neutrons for a total atomic mass of 12. There is also C13 (6 protons + 7 neutrons), and C14 (6 protons + 8 neutrons). C12 and C13 are stable, meaning that they're not prone to radioactive decay. C14, on the other hand, is radioactive. It will decay with a half life of around 5730 years. That means that every 5730 years, half of what you had will remain. In other words, starting off with 100%, in 5730 years you'll have 50%. In another 5730 years, you'll have half of that, 25%. In another 5730 years, you'll have half of that, 12.5%. This goes on and on until the number of individual atoms gets so small that such probabilistic predictions aren't as useful, anymore. ABOVE SOURCE: Nov. 21 – Halflife and Fission The reason there's C14 in the atmosphere even though it decays is primarily due to cosmic rays. When a cosmic ray impacts a nitrogen-14 (N14) atom in the upper atmosphere, it converts the N14 into an atom of C14. Then, as this C14 diffuses throughout the rest of the atmosphere, it can combine with oxygen to form carbon dioxide (CO2), and eventually get taken up by a plant during photosynthesis. This process has been more or less constant over the past several millennia, so the ratios of C12:C13:C14 have also been more or less constant*. ABOVE SOURCE: SkepticalScience.com - Carbon 14 origin , under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Although the chemistry of photosynthesis is somewhat biased towards using the lighter isotopes of carbon, plants still take up all of the isotopes, and in proportions that are roughly consistent across all the different kinds of plants (and not too far off from the proportions in the atmosphere – though enough to be measurable). And since most food webs (especially land based ones) have plants at the base, and animals are always eating and pooping and peeing to keep a near constant turnover of their carbon atoms, this same ratio of C12:C13:C14 holds throughout most living things**. However, once an organism dies, it quits taking part in this constant exchange of carbon. The ratio of isotopes will begin to measurably change as the C14 decays. So, knowing the half-life of C14, you can measure this ratio and determine how long it's been since the organism died, i.e. how old it is. (In practice, researchers mostly look at the ratio of C12:C14, and don't pay much attention to C13 – at least for carbon dating – the ratio of C12:C13 is important to environmental scientists and climatologists.) So now we can address the limitations. The first should be rather obvious from the first graph up above. By the time you get something that's been dead for over 50k years, the amount of C14 left is truly miniscule, and real life sensors are only so accurate. In other words, once you get down to such trace levels of C14, you can't expect sensors accurate enough to distinguish between a 100k year old sample and a 150k year old sample. It would be like using a tape measure to try to measure the difference between .001" and .002" – it's simply beyond the capability of the measuring device. Even if you had magic sensors that could count every single atom in a sample, you'd start running into issues of applying probabilities to small sample sizes. As an analogy, consider flipping coins. Flip a coin 1000 times, and you'll almost surely have close to half heads and half tails. Flip a coin 2 times, and 2 heads or 2 tails isn't shocking. Flip a coin 1 time, and you can't have half heads and half tails. If I did my math right, a 1g sample of carbon would contain around 5e22 atoms. Given the ratio of C12 to C14, that would be around 5.7e10 (57 trillion) C14 atoms. With a half life of 5730 years, the math works out to 1.65 atoms in just over 200,000 years. Obviously, you can't have 1.65 atoms. But more fundamentally, at such small sample sizes, you don't know if an individual atom will decay tomorrow, or in another 100,000 years. So when you're left with just a handful of atoms, random chance can outweigh probability. ABOVE SOURCE: Me and Excel And there's another problem on top of that. Just because most of the C14 comes from cosmic rays doesn't mean that all of it does. Cosmic rays aren't the only source of the high energy particles that can convert N14 into C14. The decay of the uranium-thorium isotope series also releases such particles that can accomplish the same conversion. And since there are trace levels of uranium basically throughout the entire planet, along with deposits with higher concentrations, this process will occur pretty much everywhere. In living and relatively recently deceased organisms, the trace amounts of C14 from such other sources is dwarfed by that from the atmosphere, so that the effect on dating is negligible. But once a sample is old enough that most of the C14 that originally came from the atmosphere has already decayed, that sample will still contain newly created C14 from background radiation. Or alternatively, even objects that were never alive and never had any atmospheric C14 could have some level of C14 from these other sources. So, those are the issues with trying to apply carbon dating to objects older than around 50k years. I mean, sure, you can go through the procedures, and an algorithm might even spit out a number. But that number is meaningless. It doesn't really tell you anything about the age of such an object. You certainly can’t get a meaningful number from carbon dating*** for an object millions of years old. *By calibrating carbon dating to other dating methods like tree ring counting, researchers discovered that the ratios of C12:C13:C14 weren't exactly constant over the past tens of thousands of years, allowing them to come up with calibration curves to give more precise dates. **Certain ecosystems, such as those deep underwater in the ocean, are more isolated from atmospheric C14, and so may have different ratios. So you should only apply carbon dating to samples from organisms that lived in or near the atmosphere. ***Thankfully, there are other radioisotope dating methods, but these are applied to igneous or volcanic rocks and ash, and so date the sediment above and below objects of interest, not the objects themselves. Different radioactive substances with different half lives have different useful ranges.

Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes? Back when I was in college, I bought a somewhat decent mountain bike* to get around. I didn't give a whole lot of thought to mountain bike vs. road bike at the time. I mean, mountain bikes just sounded cooler, and it seemed that a mountain bike would be more robust to the abuse of daily riding, jumping curbs, hitting potholes, and the like. It was fine, got me to and from campus, and I even took it on a nearby trail a handful of times. Riding a bike daily like that for over 2 years got me pretty accustomed to cycling. Fast forward a few years to living in Wichita Falls, Texas, and we have a huge cycling event known as the Hotter'n Hell Hundred, so named for a 100 mile route in potentially 100°F weather (though it now takes place in the morning and so isn't usually quite that hot). A group of us decided to participate one year just to say we did it, but sticking with a shorter 25 mile route. One friend was really into cycling, so he offered to go down to a place in Dallas to pick up good road bike rentals for the weekend – bikes up in the several thousand dollar range if we were going to buy them. ABOVE: The Mass Start at the Hotter'n Hell Hundred SOURCE: 40th Hotter 'N Hell Hundred event photos When I first got up on that road bike and pressed down on the pedal... Wow! The bike just glided across the pavement like it was nothing. And when I stopped pedaling, the bike didn't stop. It just kept on coasting and coasting seemingly forever. There was just no comparison between that road bike and the mountain bike that I'd ridden back in college. The road bike was supremely optimized to be low friction for riding on pavement. Now, I'm still not sure a road bike would have been the best option for me in college with the amount I abused my bike. And there's no way I would have been able to shell out several thousands of dollars for a road bike comparable to that one I rented. But after riding a good road bike when all I was used to before was a mountain bike, I can definitely understand why people opt for road bikes. I mean, it’s in the name. That’s what they’re designed for. *My bike in college was a Raleigh M50 - looked just like this: 2000 Raleigh M50 Front Suspension Mountain Bike for Sale in Mechanicsburg, PA - OfferUp. If memory serves, it cost somewhere around $300 back in the 90s, which would be the equivalent of around $600 today. So not a world class bike, but definitely better than what you find in a typical Walmart.

What was your initial reaction to learning about evolution in school? Did you immediately believe it or did you have doubts about its validity? It was a revelation. Prior to that, my exposure to evolution was pop-science articles or the way it was casually discussed in nature documentaries. And while those treat evolution as a given, and may even discuss evolutionary relationships, they hardly ever go into detail of the mechanisms or how evolution actually works. So, like many folks, I had a more Lamarckian view of evolution, of use and disuse and even intentionality on the parts of organisms. I remember one example in particular that left me dumbfounded, of a symbiotic relationship between certain plant and ant species, where the plants provided food and shelter for the ants in exchange for the ants protecting the plants. How could either one of them have intentionally initiated such a relationship? How could organisms with such little to no cognitive ability do anything intentional at all? ABOVE SOURCE: Ecological and Evolutionary Responses of Protective Ant-Plant Mutualisms to Environmental Changes (Chapter 11) - Ant-Plant Interactions When I was finally formally taught the mechanisms of mutation and natural selection, it all fell into place. You don't need any intention. Mutations are just mistakes on a mechanical level, so diversity is inevitable. And as soon as you have diversity, differential reproduction is also inevitable. Evolution didn't just make sense. There was simply no way it couldn't happen. Even my ant-plant example finally made sense. All you needed was some type of mutation on a plant to attract certain ants, and given ants' aggressive behaviors, that would protect the plants from other organisms that might try to eat them. And from there, additional mutations just refine the relationship further. So while I might have said that I already accepted evolution prior to my high school biology class, I didn't actually understand it. By learning how evolution actually works, that class made me much more certain in the truth of evolution. I still had a period of minor doubt a few years later when Intelligent Design was at its peak popularity, wondering if I was being a good Christian when so many other Christians insisted you had to accept some form of creationism. So I researched evolution even deeper than that high school biology class, and given that the evidence really is overwhelming, I only became more certain of evolution. (I might add, that while it's certainly possible to be a Christian and accept evolution, this incident was one of the stimuli to start me on the path to atheism.)
