It’s almost exactly like that. Anybody can write out a check purported to be worth $1 billion. But as soon as you try to cash the check, it will bounce, and you’ll realize it was just an empty promise or even an intentional lie or scam. And your bank might even charge you a fee for their inconvenience. You’ll have gotten your hopes up, only to be in the same financial situation or maybe even a little bit worse than before you received this check. If a random person offers you a $1 billion check, my advice is that you refuse to cash it. Of course, in the case of an afterlife, once you die and cease to exist, you won’t realize that it was an empty promise or a scam. But if there are strings attached (and with religions, there usually are), you’ll still have wasted at least some opportunities in the one life we actually do get.

Why does my keyboard have a caps lock key? It must have some purpose, right? This is a good question. Is there really a need for a caps lock key on modern keyboards? How many times do most people use it intentionally, vs. eNDING UP WITH SENTENCES UNINTENTIONALLY WRITTEN IN ALL CAPS? The obvious function is that it lets you write in all caps, LIKE THIS, without having to hold down the shift key. This stems from old, mechanical typewriters, where the shift key actually did mechanically shift the typing mechanism to switch between lower case and upper case letters, which required a decent amount of force on the key. So, for prolonged all caps typing, a shift-lock locked the mechanism in the shifted position, easing the load on your pinky fingers. But shift-lock shifted all the keys, including the symbols on numbers, so a slightly later innovation was caps-lock that only shifted the letters, not the entire keyboard. Once electric typewriters, word processors, and early computers came around, the effort to hold down shift wasn’t nearly so hard, but it was still nice to have a caps-lock key. Remember that typewriters and early printers (like Daisy wheels) still didn’t allow for much formatting or different font sizes, so all-caps was still a convenient way to distinguish things like titles and headings. But on modern day computers? Just about any serious project that needs to be in all-caps can be handled by software, and in many cases, it’s even preferable to do it that way. For example, for headings in a paper, you should type them out in normal mixed case, e.g. Heading Example. Then, if you want it in all caps, just change the heading style to all caps, and the word processing software will take care of it for you. But if you decide later to switch back to mixed case, it’s just a quick change of the style rather than re-typing everything. In my own field, technical drawings use all caps as the standard for drawing annotations, but this can also be handled through software settings instead of using caps-lock (e.g. Displaying Annotation Notes in Uppercase). Even typing here on Quora, there are already a basic text formatting options. Adding an all-caps to that would be simple. There may be some niche applications, like programming, where caps-lock still has a bit of use, but I imagine a lot of that’s driven by complacency. Remove the caps-lock key from the keyboard, and programming software would pretty quickly include software features*. The more I think about it, the more I’d like to see the caps-lock key done away with, to free up that space on the keyboard for something more useful. Maybe replace it with a keyboard shortcut to enable all caps (like alt-shift-c), or at least relegate it to a far corner of the keyboard where you’re less likely to hit it by accident. Here’s something related I found doing a bit of googling: *I’m only a novice programmer, with most of my experience in Visual Basic (which just earned me several snorts of derision from the real programmers). But even back in VB 6, I only worried about capitalization when I declared my variables. After that, I typed them in all lower case, and VB would automatically convert them to the capitalization from when they were declared. Not only did it save me the effort of pressing the shift key, it was a nice, quick double check that I typed in the correct variable name (if it didn’t update capitalization, I’d made a typo).

Why should childless Americans pay for other people's kids to attend school? Well, the obvious one, like so many other people have already said, is that education contributes to the overall well being of society. Here’s one such graph, showing learning outcomes vs. GDP per capita. Note the positive correlation, and that better education corresponds to better GDP per capita. And of course, better GDP per capita is better for everybody, since that means more money in everybody’s pockets for buying goods and services to support everyone else. If you want the USA to be successful overall (or substitute your country of choice if you’re not American), then you’ll contribute your share of the investment in education. ABOVE SOURCE: Average learning outcomes vs. GDP per capita More philosophically, I think people need to think less in terms of children 'belonging' to parents. Children are citizens and residents in their own right. The government has an obligation to children as individuals, not just thinking of them as subordinates of their parents. All citizens and residents deserve a free public education. I'd wager that you received one yourself, and I know for certain that the option was at least available if you grew up in the U.S. So think of paying taxes for public education as just a delayed repayment of your own education. So all of us taxpayers pay our part to support public education, because it's for the overall good of the country, and because a free public education is something that every American is entitled to regardless of who their parents are.

Why is the Francesinha the world's best sandwich? This question contains a fallacy, and so it can’t be answered as asked. Now, I’d never heard of the Francesinha before coming across this question. So if you’re like me and had similarly never heard of it, here’s what this dish looks like: And admittedly, that does look pretty darn good. But I’m also not going to call it a sandwich. Sandwiches are meant to be eaten with your hands. That’s kind of the whole point from the very earliest times when the Earl of Sandwich invented them. If you need a knife and a fork to eat a food, that’s not a sandwich. I mean, you could put your bacon in between your French toast, but that wouldn’t make it a sandwich. So however good a Francesinha might taste, it can’t take the title for world’s best sandwich*. So what is the best sandwich? Man, there are just way too many choices to narrow it down to one. You’ve got everything from hoagies to BLTs to Reubens to club sandwiches to Bánh mì to panini to tortas to cheesesteaks to Primanti’s and on and on and on. Heck, on a cold day after playing out in the snow, a simple grilled cheese with a bowl of tomato soup can’t be beat. If Adam and Eve were indeed the 1st humans on Earth, theoretically, what’s the fastest they could populate the Earth to today's level? Theoretically in what sense? If you account for enough factors, then certainly no faster than we actually achieved our current population, and probably quite a bit slower. Basically, if you use realistic assumptions for fertility rates and mortality rates for various eras based on the conditions and medical knowledge of the times, then starting with the same initial conditions, your theoretical population growth will match the actual historical population growth. But those initial conditions are where the differences come in between reality and Biblical literalists. Here's an estimate of the global population going back several thousand years: ABOVE SOURCE: Global population 10,000BCE-2100 | Statista Per Biblical literalists, Adam and Eve would have been alive around 4000 BC. The estimates I've seen for the actual population back then range from around 7 million to 50 million. So, to get to our current population in 6000 years with realistic assumptions on fertility and mortality rates, you need a starting population in the millions. Adam and Eve were only two people. That's, well, a magnitude of around a million times less than reality. Now maybe mortality rates wouldn't be quite as bad with less people. Maybe pandemics wouldn't be as common with lower population densities. Maybe there would have been fewer famines with different environments not being pushed to their carrying capacities. Maybe there would have been less wars because of reduced conflicts over resources. So just maybe, an initial population of two people (with no genetic defects) could grow faster on a percentage basis than a population of several million and eventually catch up to the historical reality. But there's no way they could get there faster. And once the Adam and Eve hypothetical line does catch up to reality, then they'd have all the same limits on growth and causes of mortality as real historical populations. If by 'theoretical', you're ignoring realistic mortality rates, and wondering how quickly a population could grow if unconstrained by such considerations, well, that would be exponential growth, so the answer is pretty quick. For a rough calculation, if you assume that each couple has 4 surviving children that go on to have children of their own, and that generation times average 20 years, then population would double every 20 years. So, population can be calculated as 2^n, where n is the number of generations. It would take 22 generations to reach 8.6 billion people, or 440 years. But that's really more 'hypothetical' than 'theoretical', since the calculation is based on poor assumptions. So 'theoretically', as long as you're using good assumptions in your theory, if you start from a population of just 2 people 6 thousand years ago, then the population in that scenario would certainly lag the real world population for at least some period of time. Most likely, this lag would mean that it would take longer to get to our current population. But even if a reduced population allowed for reduced mortality rates, once the hypothetical population did catch up to reality, then mortality rates would be the same, and population growth would play out the same way as reality from then on out.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? Well, the story obviously isn't real. We know it developed from earlier Sumerian versions of the myth, and that even the Bible version is a blending of the Yahwist and Priestly versions of the story, with conflicting details right within the Biblical narrative. There's no archaeological evidence of such an event. And so, so many details are so ridiculously implausible that there's no way it could have happened as told in the Bible. So, right off the bat, playing a hypothetical game of 'what if', you're already having to make plenty of concessions or adjustments to try to bring the story into the realm of reality. So the question is, how fast and loose do you play with the details of the story to pretend that it’s real. If you want to include all animal species that couldn't have survived a worldwide flood, then it's just flat out impossible. Just consider how many different species there are of beetles, nematodes, ants, etc. And keep in mind that even plenty of aquatic organisms require specific conditions that wouldn't have existed in the flood waters, and so the ark would have required aquariums for those animals, as well. There's a very good article written all the way back in 1983, The Impossible Voyage of Noah's Ark, where somebody did take the time to try to figure out the actual implications of carrying every animal species. They determined the ark would have needed to hold a grand total of 3,858,920 animals. They also determined that the ark would have had 1,063,125 cubic feet of usable internal space (after accounting for structure), which would have left just 0.275 cubic feet of space for each individual animal. Sure, plenty of those animals were small, but they still need room to move around. And you still need their food on top of that. And provisions to access their enclosures for waste removal. Etc. In other words, this scenario is just flat out impossible. But creationists have a trick they like to use, pointing out that the Bible didn't use the word 'species', but 'kind', which they like to define as roughly equivalent to the genus level. In this view, for example, Noah wouldn't have had to take wolves, dogs, foxes, coyotes, and all the other canids. He could have just taken a breeding pair of the canine kind. And then after the flood, their descendants would go on to 'adapt' (because they can't use the word 'evolve') into all the different canids alive today. Of course, that would require a form of hyper-evolution much faster than anything that ever happens in reality. But it lets them come up with a semi-plausible hand-wavy explanation to save a literal reading of the myth (semi-plausible in the same way that getting bitten by a radioactive spider gives you spider powers). A good review of such an explanation using 'kinds' can be found here, Noah's Ark: A Feasibility Study (written back in 1996 – we're not talking cutting edge science required to debunk creationist nonsense). This article addressed what was essentially a feasibility study by John Woodmorappe based on these creative assumptions. Woodmorappe's estimate brought the number of animals down to a somewhat more manageable total of 'just' 15,754. This wouldn't actually be enough animals even to save every kind, but I already said we'd have to bend reality in some places to answer this hypothetical, so we'll just roll with it. So this scenario provides 67.5 cubic feet per animal. Consider that a small elephant requires 214 cubic feet of space for transport (not long term living), and that most animals will be much, much smaller, so this scenario does look like it's plausible to at least cram all the animals aboard. But even then, if you look to modern zoos, and the various requirements for actual long term living space, food storage, food preparation, waste removal, etc., there's still no way that you could keep that many animals alive in that type of space for that length of time (40 days per the Yahwist source, 150 days per the Priestly source). So to sum it all up, the answer is no. It's just flat out impossible if you're considering every single species of animal. And even if you play word games with 'kinds', while it might be physically possible to cram that many bodies aboard the ark, it wouldn't be under survivable conditions, or with anywhere near enough supplies to support the animals until the flood waters subsided. What are the units of Einstein’s mass energy equivalence equation E=mc^2? If E were in Joules what would m be? If m were in ng what would E be? Or is there some weird mathematical black magic that makes the units completely unrelatable to normies? Metric only has 7 fundamental units that get defined relative to some standard. Every other unit is derived from these seven: Really, we could use just those 7 units for everything and not have any other units. For example, we define speed as m/s without giving it a special unit. But for simple convenience, we have defined additional units based on those fundamental units, and then given them their own name for shorthand. Relevant to this question, Joules are defined as: J = kg·m²/s² Because there are many of these derived units, you can do conversions between them. Force, for example, gets the derived unit of Newtons, which are defined as follows (which is easy to remember as long as you remember F=ma): N = kg·m/s² And if you look back to the definition of Joules, it should be obvious that you can swap out kg·m/s² for N and get: J = kg·m²/s² J = (kg·m/s²)·m J = N·m It's still the equivalent to kg·m²/s² and still means the same thing. It's just a slightly shorter way to write it. Anyway, looking to Einstein's famous equation: E=mC² E=kg·(m/s)² E=kg·m²/s² E=J So, all the units work out just fine, no black magic required. And for what it's worth, since I'm an engineer in the U.S. and industry standard here is the US Customary System, the equation works just fine with those units, as well. Keeping in mind that a pound force is defined as slug·ft/s² (using the same F=ma), and that the typical unit of energy in USCS is ft·lb, you can run through the units with Einstein's equation: E=mC² E=slug·(ft/s)² E=slug·ft²/s² E=ft·(slug·ft/s²) E=ft·lb Such unit systems are known as 'consistent' systems, where you can go through all this math with the units and have things work out properly. Metric and the foot–pound–second subset of USCS obviously work fine. But there are other consistent systems out there, such as the centimetre–gram–second system or the inch-slinch-second system. For USCS, there's a whole panoply of non-consistent units that require conversion before you start on the real math (like converting BTUs to ft·lb). For metric, you mostly only have to worry about time, making sure everything's done in seconds and not minutes or hours (e.g. km/h is not an official SI unit, neither is Wh for energy). But as long as you do stick with consistent units, all your math in science and engineering will work out just fine.

If atheists begin to believe in my god, what would they lose? They will not lose anything. Do you think there is a unique atheist approach to morality, or do atheists simply adhere to the same moral code as everyone else? I'd actually put it the other way around. I think that religious folks, despite often paying lip service to their religion or taking a few superficial rules from their scriptures, actually develop their moral code the same way as everyone else. Do you really need the Bible telling you that murder is wrong to avoid wanting to kill people? I don't mean in a 'ha-ha' hyperbolic sort of way, but the thought of literally taking somebody's life and living with that on your conscience. For most people, being averse to murder is just a part of human nature, independent of whatever religion they were raised in or lack thereof. On the other hand, do you agree that it's immoral to sell your daughter into slavery? Or simply to own slaves in general? Probably, even though the Bible says those things are perfectly fine. It merely sets some rules around those practices to keep them from becoming excessively bad, but even the New Testament has a passage instructing slaves to be loyal to their masters - 1 Peter 2:18. So, where do people get morality? It's a combination of innate instincts and human nature in things like empathy and fairness, built upon by social mores that we learn as we grow up, and perhaps even a bit of philosophy for the people who think about it a lot. If you're raised in a religious community, you may acquire the specific social mores of that community, but it's still the same general process as folks outside that community.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? There are two aspects of this answer. First, of course teaching creationism in public schools violates the separation of church and state in the U.S. This has repeatedly been the interpretation of courts, from Epperson v. Arkansas back in 1968 to the more recent Kitzmiller v. Dover Area School District in 2005 (Ten Major Court Cases about Evolution and Creationism). But that's only a legal technicality. What if we didn't have the First Amendment, or lived in a different country that didn't enshrine the separation of church and state? Well, then we have the much more fundamental issue that creationism is wrong. I don't think many people realize that creationism was the dominant scientific paradigm prior to Darwin. Some naturalists may have toyed with ideas of 'transmutation', but they were largely seen as fringe eccentrics. At best, some naturalists were more in line with certain modern day creationists who concede evolution within 'kinds', but not universal common descent. It was the plausible theory and especially the evidence that Darwin presented in The Origin that basically convinced the scientific community practically overnight to accept evolution over creationism. In other words, those naturalists didn't reject creationism because they were a priori opposed to it, but because the evidence conclusively favored evolution over creationism. And in the 150+ years since then, the evidence for evolution has only grown even more overwhelming. So yes, teaching creationism in public schools in the U.S. would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. But even more importantly, creationism is factually incorrect and not good science, so why would you want to teach it to our children in the first place?

What are the scientific odds of human existence? What conditions are necessary for life to exist? That's a very interesting question (the first one). The late Stephen Jay Gould came up with a thought experiment of 'rewinding' the history of life and starting over. Would you get the same results? How much of evolution is driven by randomness and chance, how much is driven by contingency, and how much is driven by more general principles? Here's how Gould himself put it: Suppose that ten of a hundred designs will survive and diversify. If the ten survivors are predictable by superiority of anatomy (Interpretation 1), then they will win each time – and Burgess eliminations do not challenge our comforting view of life. But if the ten survivors are protégés of Lady Luck or fortunate beneficiaries of odd historical contingencies (Interpretation 2), then each replay of the tape will yield a different set of survivors and a radically different history. And if you recall from high-school algebra how to calculate permutations and combinations, you will realize that the total number of combinations for 10 items from a pool of 100 yields more than 17 trillion potential outcomes. There's one particular experiment that comes as close as I can think of to replaying the tape of life, in the small scale, at least*. Back in 1988, Richard Lenski started out with one strain of E. coli, and split it into 12 different populations. He grew each population in identical conditions (well, as close to identical as experimentally possible) which were actually somewhat harsh for E. coli. He used a particular growth medium named DM25, which has a limited amount of glucose that the E. coli need to feed on. Lenski wanted to see how the E. coli would evolve due to this limited food supply. Every day, he would transfer 1% of the previous day's populations to new flasks with a fresh supply of DM25, periodically freezing samples to maintain as a kind of 'fossil record', and also periodically measuring attributes of the populations to see how they were evolving. The experiment is still ongoing today, making it one of the longest running (and supremely well documented) evolutionary experiments. Here's how one particular trait evolved in each of these populations, cell size: ABOVE SOURCE: E. coli long-term evolution experiment - Wikipedia While there's a general trend of increasing cell size in all 12 populations, they didn't all follow the exact same trend. In fact, the largest lineage evolved to be nearly twice as big as the smallest lineage. One particular adaptation was so rare that it only occurred in one of Lenski's populations.* The DM25 growth medium also happened to contain a large amount of citrate, which E. coli usually can't digest in anaerobic conditions, but which was included in the DM25 formulation way back when it was first developed for antibiotic experiments because it improved the efficiency of penicillin. Well, in this single lineage of Lenski's twelve E. coli populations, they did evolve the ability to digest citrate in anaerobic conditions. This adaptation is so profound for E. coli that some have proposed it actually represents a new species. So, starting from identical genetics, and subjecting populations to as identical of conditions as experimentally possible, each of the 12 populations took their own different evolutionary paths, from cell size, to the ability to digest citrate, to other traits I didn't mention here. There wasn't simply one optimum set of adaptations that natural selection drove towards in each population. This really does seem to indicate that chance† and contingency are major factors in the evolution of populations. And Lenski's experiment only had 12 isolated populations. What if he'd had 100? Would there be 100 unique strains by now? What about 1000? Or a million? Or to put it into the terminology of this question, what are the scientific odds of any particular strain of E. coli evolving in any particular flask? Based on Lenski's experiment, we can say it's no greater than 1 out of 12, but the reality could be a much, much smaller probability. So, let that play out in every population that's ever existed, and it seems that every particular species has a very low probability of existing‡. That goes for everything from ocelots to dandelions to Humboldt's squid to portabella mushrooms. And yes, it goes for us humans, as well. To add one more thing, it does seem like some body plans or adaptations are more common than others, implying that there are general principles that drive these adaptations. Levers to propel an organism on the seafloor or land, aka legs, have evolved in animals as diverse as insects, tetrapods, and starfish. Free swimming organisms evolved streamlined hydrodynamic bodies. Flying animals evolve wings. Etc. But other adaptations appear to be quite rare, like Lenski's citrate digesting E. coli. If elephants were to go extinct, I'm not sure we'd ever see another animal with that kind of trunk. And I can only hope that when aye-ayes go extinct, that particular combination of nightmare fuel never reappears. I rather suspect that we humans are kind of like elephants in that respect. You simply don't see many other animals similar to us outside our closest evolutionary cousins. We have a weird combination of an upright bipedal posture, complex social groups, extremely high intelligence with a penchant for technology combined with hands that are really good at manipulating our environments to effect that technology, along with several other unique characteristics. So, outside the general principle of all particular species being highly improbable, I'd say that even a species along the lines of us humans is highly improbable. Play the tape of life 1000 times, and while you might get lots of critters superficially resembling a crab, you might not get another elephant or another human. While I'm not sure anybody can give the precise odds, I think it's safe to say that the odds of human existence were quite low. So much of evolution is driven by chance and contingency, and we seem to be a rather odd combination of traits on top of that. That's all the more reason we need to get our acts together and make sure we don't screw up our planet (whether through things like climate change or good old fashioned global thermonuclear war). Because if we do go extinct, the odds are decent that nothing with our ability for science and understanding will ever evolve on this planet, again. *Both of these paragraphs are mostly copied from a previous answer of mine: †Chance could be things like Genetic drift or even the raw material of random mutation. ‡Don't confuse low probabilities of a particular species with low probabilities of life in general. A common analogy is shuffling a deck of cards. With 52 unique cards, the odds of any particular order for an entire deck is 1 in 10^68, an astronomically tiny probability. But, you're essentially guaranteed some order of 52 cards. That's the way it is with evolution and species – the odds of any particular species may be infinitesimally small, but the evolution of species in general is pretty much guaranteed. Argh. If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from? This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.

Is reheating leftovers in a microwave good or bad? It depends on the food and your own taste buds. For me, they're fine for 'wet' foods, like mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, soups, etc. They're not so great for foods that need a crunchy or dry texture, like the breading on fried chicken, or the crust of a pizza. Microwaves tend to make such foods soggy, and, in my opinion, worse than just eating those foods cold. If you feel the need to reheat foods like that, you're better off using an oven, convection oven, or stovetop. If you're somehow worried about health risks because microwaves emit electromagnetic radiation, just remember that a light bulb also emits electromagnetic radiation. Microwaves are just a longer wavelength than visible light, which works out better for penetrating a bit more beneath the surface of food to excite the water molecules to heat them up. But a sufficiently powerful light bulb (or better yet, a heat lamp) will also heat up food just from visible light. Microwaves are no more dangerous to your food than shining a flashlight onto it or eating food in broad daylight. ABOVE: Microwaves are actually lower energy waves than visible light. It's the other end of the electromagnetic spectrum, with x-rays and gamma rays, where you have to worry about ionizing radiation SOURCE: Electromagnetic Spectrum - Introduction So, for the right kinds of food, microwaves do just fine for re-heating.

If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it? Before getting into the why, let's get a little perspective. Here is the breakdown of global religious affiliation: SOURCE: The Changing Global Religious Landscape That's a lot of diversity of religions, and none of them are believed by a majority of the world's population. And since many of these religions are mutually contradictory, it stands to reason that most of them are wrong. So, your question isn't just applicable to Christianity. It's applicable to all religions. Why do people believe them, when logically, most of them must be wrong? A big reason is the cognitive bias that Deborah Kelemen has coined 'promiscuous teleology', which is a tendency to see purpose and intention even when it's not really there. Here's an explanation from one paper on the topic, Teleology and the intentions of supernatural agents: Given that according to PT [promiscuous teleology], teleological reasoning develops from an early understanding of intentionality which is then overextended (Kelemen, 1999a), the notion of agency is central to teleology. This is because the only things capable of having intentions are things with minds, and the only things with minds are agents. In this view, just as “chairs are for sitting on” is true only if an agent intends the chair to serve this function, the statement “clouds rain so that plants can grow” is based in the misbelief that plants growing is the intended function of the cloud raining. The difference between these two teleological explanations is that whereas the former implies the intentions of a natural agent (a human), the latter seems to imply the intentions of a supernatural agent. And here's the abstract from a different paper, Promiscuous Teleology: From Childhood Through Adulthood and from West to East: From infancy we continually try to make sense of what goes on around us. One strategy in making sense of things is to look for how things might be purposeful or designed. So useful is this strategy that sometimes it gets overused—what Deborah Keleman calls promiscuous teleology . This chapter reviews research with children and adults across cultures—including recent work in China —that demonstrates that promiscuous teleology is a conceptual default that all peoples share but that may be tamped down through enculturation. Kelemen argues that this teleological reasoning makes certain religious ideas about supernatural agents’ activity in creating or ordering the world largely intuitive. Or to summarize all that, our tendency to see agency everywhere makes us prone to supernatural explanations. Now, there are further questions as to why we might have evolved this cognitive bias in the first place. As I noted in another answer, "There are various explanations for why we might have evolved this bias – from being social animals and having to understand intentions of our fellow humans, to being prodigious tool makers and having an instinctual sense of 'function' for items. And there's no reason the explanations need to be mutually exclusive. (And even all that is assuming it's an adaptive trait, and not just a spandrel of San Marco.)" Add in how children credulously accept lessons from their parents (and understandably so – there's too much knowledge to pass down any other way), and culture, and how these stories morph and change over the generations, and you've got the perfect recipe for a large diversity of supernatural stories to explain various aspects of our world. Christianity just happens to be one of these myths among many.

What is the biggest flying vertebrate of all time? Given the incompleteness of the fossil record in general, the fragmentary remains of certain species in particular, and the vagaries of trying to reconstruct an entire animal based solely on fossil skeletal remains, the best answer can only be an estimate, not definitive. There are still a few standouts worth discussing, all of them pterosaurs, and all within one particular family, the Azhdarchidae. ABOVE: From left to right – a typical person for comparison, Quetzalcoatlus northropi, Arambourgiania philadelphiae, Hatzegopteryx thambema, and Cryodrakon boreas; note that these reconstructions are not based on the most complete of remains CREDIT: Gabriel Ugueto SOURCE: https://malibestsk.xyz/product_details/22449788.html Quetzalcoatlus northropi Q. northropi may be the most well known of these. When I was growing up, Quetzalcoatlus was the undisputed king of flying vertebrates before those other fossils had been discovered (or at least properly identified – Cryodrakon was originally misidentified as a Quetzalcoatlus species). Unfortunately, as Mark Witton put it in the article, Quetzalcoatlus: the media concept vs. the science, "It's also only known from bits and pieces of a gigantic left wing and cannot be regarded as a well known animal." Reconstructions of Q. northropi are instead based on comparisons to its smaller cousin, Q. lawsoni (referred to as Q. sp in older literature before it was finally named in 2021) – we have found much more complete remains of that species. As such, many estimates are based on scaling up Q. lawsoni to the size of the wing bones found for Q. northropi. ABOVE: Doug Lawson holding the massive humerus of Q. northropi SOURCE: The Quetz Monograph Lives and Other News on Azhdarchid Pterosaurs — Tetrapod Zoology Anyway, referring to that same Mark Witton article, "recent estimates of its wingspan being in the region of 10 m [32.8 ft] and predicted body masses of 200-260 kg [440-575 lbs]." Arambourgiania philadelphiae There are only very fragmentary remains of this animal. Here's a diagram from Mark Witton to show just how little. Only the parts in white are known from actual remains – one neck vertebrae and a few fragments from the wing. The parts in gray are conjecture. Note that A. philadelphiae is the creature on the right, while Q. lawsoni (the smaller Quetzalcoatlus species) is shown on the left for comparison: ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on left, A. philadelphia on right SOURCE: Why the giant azhdarchid Arambourgiania philadelphiae needs a fanclub If you look at the Wikipedia description of the animal, you find winspan estimates anywhere from 7-13 m (23-43 ft), though many pterosaur experts feel the higher side is an overestimate. In that same article from Mark Witton that I pulled the above figure from, he made a casual comment of a body mass in the range of 200-250 kg (440-550 lbs). Hatzegopteryx thambema Hatzegopteryx is know from a bit more fossil material. Here's a similar figure to the one above, which includes this species. It includes Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center. The figure uses the same conventions of white for known material, and gray for conjecture. 2BNaish%2Band%2BWitton%2B2016.jpg ABOVE: Q. lawsoni on the left, A. philadelphiae on the right, and H. thambema front and center SOURCE: New paper: when the short-necked, giant azhdarchid pterosaur Hatzegopteryx ruled Late Cretaceous Romania These bones show Hatzegopteryx to have been much more robust than the other known Azhdarchids, with a much wider skull than other known Azhdarchid skulls. Combined with the fact that no large theropods are known from the sediments where the Hatzegopteryx fossils were found, this has led to the idea that it might have been an apex predator in its environment. Wingspan estimates for this creature range from 10-12 m (33-39 ft). Relying on Wikipedia for another weight estimate, it might have been somewhere between 180-250 kg (400-550 lbs). Cryodrakon boreas From the little I've been able to find about this animal, the fossil remains come from a few different individuals, including (but not limited to) a neck vertebrae from a juvenile, and another neck vertebrae from an adult comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus northropi. The Wikipedia description does state that it appears to have been slightly more robust thatn Q. northropi, so perhaps a bit heavier. ABOVE SOURCE: Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology (@RoyalTyrrell) on X So, which one of these species was actually the biggest? Who can say? The fossil remains just aren’t complete enough to say anything definitive about even the individual animals they’re from, let alone variation within each species. But it is interesting that all of them seem to be bumping up against the same limits on wingspan and bodyweight, of somewhere in the neighborhood of 10 m (33 ft) and 225 kg (500 lbs). That seems to suggest that that's approaching the limit of how big pterosaurs could get and still be able to fly. So perhaps, even if we do find more giant pterosaurs in the future, they'll still be in the same ballpark. Most of the links provided in the above answer are worth reading if you want more details. Atheists, if a 10-year-old child asks you why you don't believe in God, do you feel guilty for crushing their innocent beliefs? I have to admit, this has always seemed like a weird concept to me. It's not just religion. You see it in other types of children's stories, like Santa Claus, fairies, magic, etc. It's this idea that, not just are we supposed to indulge children in believing obvious nonsense that we as adults know isn't true, but that we're actually supposed to encourage it, because, well, I'm not entirely sure why. It never seems to be explained other than holding belief in itself as a virtue (some might say gullibility). I think a lot of adults don't give kids enough credit. By somewhere around 3 to 5 years old, children are able to distinguish reality from fantasy (Young Children Learn to Distinguish Between Fact and Fiction, Research at University of Texas at Austin Finds). That doesn't mean their imagination withers away after they turn 5, or that they quit playing make believe. They're just mature enough to know, for example, that all the ghost and goblin stories around Halloween are just fun stories we tell to scare ourselves a bit, not real things that we need to fear in real life. So, while I was still a recent 'convert' to atheism when my own daughter was young, so that I still thought of religion as a bit of a taboo subject, and I did give in a bit to societal pressure on Santa Claus and the Easter Bunny, I didn't shy away from telling her the truth about other mythical ideas like fairies or the Loch Ness monster*. (Of course, like dad's everywhere, I did take a few cues from the dad in Calvin and Hobbes, leading her on with obvious nonsense from time to time just to keep her on her toes.) It didn't stunt her imagination, because we still invented plenty of games where we had to create entire worlds that didn't actually exist inside our living room or back yard. And it's not like the real world is boring. Try teaching a seven year old about deep time and evolution, or the vastness of the universe, the sheer power of supernovae, or the incomprehensibility of quantum mechanics. Obviously, I wasn't giving my daughter super deep lessons in any of those things. But when she went through her stage of asking why, why, why, I always tried to give her as accurate of an answer as I could, tailored to something she could understand at her age. And sometimes, the answer ended with an "I don't know," which left it open as a mystery and something that she might be able to figure out. And of course, there were practical lessons, too, from the typical kitchen science experiments, to the time we dissected a squirrel that the cat had killed (my wife wasn’t exactly thrilled about that one, but since she’s a nurse and had studied anatomy, we still called her out to the back yard to help us identify everything we were seeing). It gets a bit touchy when it's somebody else's kid and not your own – not so much because I'm worried about the kid, but because I'm worried about respecting the parents and not interfering in how they're raising their own children. Even if I don't agree with them on that particular subject, it's still a touchy thing to undermine parents. But overall, I don't understand this idea that we should actively encourage children to literally believe in things that we adults know aren't true. Past around 5 years old, kids are perfectly capable of separating fact from fiction, and realizing that the worlds they create in their imaginations are fantasy, not reality. But that doesn't stop them from creating those fantasy worlds. If anything, the scenario proposed in this question is an indictment on the kid's parents, for letting the kid believe in a fantasy to such a late age. By 10 years old, kids should already have a decent idea of what's real and what's pretend, so there shouldn't be any possibility of 'crushing' their beliefs. *If I had it to do over again, I wouldn't have pussy-footed around religion. And I would have treated Santa like Halloween – a game of make believe that we'd all participate in, not something to lie to her about or mislead her.

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.

Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

Evolutionists have been debating the chicken and chicken egg question for a long time. Can evolution explain which came first? No, because evolution helps us to understand that it's not the type of thing you can pinpoint. It would be like trying to define the precise second when dusk becomes night, or the precise date that a child becomes an adult. It just doesn't work that way. These are gradual processes that elude precise demarcations. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. In sexually reproducing animals, there's no single individual that's a different species from their parents, or indeed, the entire population of which they're a part. Plus, there's plenty of genetic variability within a population, which will be recombined in all types of different ways as the animals mate. So you can't even pick an individual organism as the first chicken, after which all of its descendants will subsequently be chickens, as that individual and its descendants will still have to mate with other members of the population, continuing to mix up those genes. Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? Yes, but a couple clarifications, first. First, it's not like any fish personally decided to grow limbs that were closer to legs than fins. Mutation really is a random process beyond the conscious control of the organisms experiencing those mutations. Just think about yourself. Did you choose any of the genetic mutations that differentiate you from your parents? If you have any children, did you choose any of the genetic mutations that got passed on to them? No, of course not. Such mutations are things that happen on a chemical level that we're never aware of. Heck, us people are just about the only organisms with the smarts to even understand genetics in the first place, so our ancient fish ancestors certainly weren't thinking about genetic mutations. Second, evolution of such big transitions is a gradual process that takes many, many generations to happen. It's not like there was a fish species that instantly evolved into a land dwelling animal, let alone into us humans. There were many stages along the way, from 'walking' underwater (similar to frogfish or certain walking sharks in the modern day), to slightly amphibious lifestyles (like some catfish), to even more amphibious lifestyles (like mudskippers), to something that's finally fully specialized for a life totally on land. Here's a diagram showing some of the stages along the fish to tetrapod transition, with some extra detail on the limbs, and how these limbs gradually went through this transition from fully aquatic to amphibious to fully terrestrial: ABOVE SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods Here's another figure to give a sense of the transition from those first tetrapods to us people. One thing that can sometimes be a bit misleading about diagrams like this is showing just a single path, perhaps giving the impression that this path was inevitably leading towards us. But you could make diagrams like this for any living creature, e.g. the path to mosquitos, the path to dandelions, or the path to a mushroom. And even in this path, at any critter on there, if you weren't specifically interested in human evolution, you could go off in a different direction to look at other creatures. For example, from Orrorin around 6 million years ago, you could go down a different path that led to chimpanzees rather than us people. Or from that Repenomamus around 230 million years ago, you could pick paths to any mammal alive today. Is the platypus related to dinosaurs or birds in terms of evolution? All life is related through common descent. So the only question is, how closely? And that's going to depend on your perspective. So sure, in comparison to a rose bush, mammals (including platypuses) and dinosaurs are pretty closely related. If you want to look at the similarities between mammals and dinosaurs, we're both eukaryotes, then animals, then vertebrates, and then tetrapods. So we're more closely related than any organism outside of those groups. But if you're wondering if platypuses are more closely related to dinosaurs than to us, then no. Platypuses are definitely mammals. They have fur, mammary glands, and a host of other features firmly placing them as mammals. However, the lineage that eventually gave rise to platypuses did split off from our lineage a long time ago, before our lineage had developed several other features that we now think of as typically mammalian, such as more developed teats and live birth. So although platypuses have evolved in their own way since the split, they've retained the ancestral condition on things like laying eggs and having a cloaca. Now, there is one other feature of platypuses that sometimes confuses people in that their snout bears a superficial resemblance to a beak, or to a duck's bill. But that really is only superficial. If you compare the skulls, you can see that the underlying structure is not at all similar. A duck's jaw is basically the same shape as the beak, with just a thin coating of keratin on top of the bone (keratin is the same substance as our fingernails). A platypus jaw is very different, and the bone is covered in soft tissue and skin to give it its characteristic shape. The snout is also covered in thousands of electroreceptors it uses to find prey underwater. And as one last note, while baby platypuses are born with teeth, those fall out by adulthood. What looks like possible molars on the skull below are actually bony plates, not teeth. ABOVE: Duck skull on left vs. platypus skull on right - there’s not really any mistaking the two SOURCES: Amazon and Skulls Unlimited, combined by me Anyway, if you want to know how closely related any two different organisms are, a great website is: You can type any two species that are within its database, and it will give an estimate (based on published research) on how long ago their last common ancestor lived. So, for platypuses and us humans, it gives an estimate of 180 million years ago. For platypuses and blue jays (to pick a dinosaur at random), it gives an estimate of 319 million years ago. (And just to be clear, since platypuses are mammals just like us, our last common ancestor with blue jays was also 319 million years ago.) And since I mentioned it up in the beginning, the last common ancestor between all of us animals and a rose bush was around 1.53 billion years ago. So, even though our last common ancestor with a platypus was a long time ago, the last common ancestor with dinosaurs was even longer ago than that, and that last common ancestor with a rose bush was much, much longer ago than even that. What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Well Quora Prompt Generator, this is actually a good question. While some of the strongest modern day evidence we have for evolution lies in DNA and the fossil record, DNA wasn't available at all to Darwin, and the fossil record wasn't anywhere near so well known, so Darwin had to rely on other forms of evidence to understand evolution and natural selection. You can get a quick overview just by looking at the titles of the chapters in his landmark book, On the Origin of Species: 1. VARIATION UNDER DOMESTICATION. 2. VARIATION UNDER NATURE. 3. STRUGGLE FOR EXISTENCE. 4. NATURAL SELECTION. 5. LAWS OF VARIATION. 6. DIFFICULTIES ON THEORY. 7. INSTINCT. 8. HYBRIDISM. 9. ON THE IMPERFECTION OF THE GEOLOGICAL RECORD. 10. ON THE GEOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF ORGANIC BEINGS. 11. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION. 12. GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION—continued. 13. MUTUAL AFFINITIES OF ORGANIC BEINGS: MORPHOLOGY: 14. RECAPITULATION AND CONCLUSION. In the first two chapters about variation, Darwin was looking at existing animals. One of his insights was the arbitrary distinction between 'varieties' and 'species', and that these distinctions weren't actually very clear cut. If species had been created separately and distinctly, you would expect identification to be straightforward. But if species were gradually morphing generation by generation, then you would run into these types of difficulties that Darwin identified. Rather than the differences in individual organisms being slight variations around a common archetype, there wasn't really any metaphysical archetype at all, nothing constraining what was 'normal' within a population or stopping the population from shifting over time. I'll also note that Darwin spent a lot of these chapters looking at pigeons, since those were a popular animal among breeders at the time, with lots of examples of different varieties and changes through breeding. The Struggle for Existence was more laying the groundwork to introduce natural selection. It seems rather obvious, now, but when you look at just how many offspring most organisms have, it's way, way more than what the environment can support (e.g. sea turtles lay hundreds of eggs each nesting season – if they all survived, the world would be quickly overrun by sea turtles). So, that necessarily means that the vast majority of organisms are killed without ever reproducing themselves, setting up an implicit competition. The fourth chapter is obviously where Darwin explicitly explained Natural Selection. Whether you want to count that as evidence or not, it was where he proposed a plausible framework for evolution. And the way science actually works in practice, you need that combination of evidence and explanatory framework to make a truly successful theory. The chapter on Laws of Variation looked once again to many types of living organisms, and the types of variation within populations – birds (and more pigeons, again), beetles, blind cave animals, various plants, etc., and especially the patterns of variation, and how those patterns were better explain by common descent than by special creation. Chapter 6 was about Difficulties on Theory. Darwin did highlight the lack of known transitional forms in the fossil record at the time. This is also the chapter that includes the statement loved by creationists, that the evolution of the eye "seems, I freely confess, absurd in the highest possible degree." However, for each of the potential difficulties he raised, he went on to offer responses and potential mitigating reasons, and still kept his conjecture based on evidence from living organisms (e.g. even though he got it a bit mixed up, highlighting the similarity of swim bladders to lungs as a potential evolutionary pathway; though in truth, lungs actually came first and evolved into swim bladders). And in the case of the fossil record, he's certainly been vindicated, as more extensive study in the century and a half since he published that book has found innumerable transitional fossils. In fact, one of the best examples, Archaeopteryx, was discovered in 1861, just 2 years after he published The Origin in 1859. Darwin himself noted that the chapter on Instinct could have been included in the previous chapter, but he decided to give it a fuller treatment. And again, his approach was to show plausible scenarios for adaptations that might at first blush seem too far fetched. He even introduced the idea of kin selection, "that selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end." The next chapter was about Hybridism, and taking a close look at fertility and infertility when hybridizing organisms from different species and varieties. This was an in-depth analysis to support his previous point of the distinction between species and varieties not being clear cut, which is what you'd expect from common descent. The next two chapters dealt with the geological record. The first of these two was a more detailed treatment of the issues raised in Chapter 6 about the incompleteness of the geological record, while explaining what was known at the time. As far as evidence, this was obviously pretty heavy on geological strata and formations. The next chapter built on that, synthesizing the facts previously laid out and introducing a few more fossils to explain how the evidence that did exist was entirely consistent with and indicative of common descent. Moreover, and perhaps based on his time on the Beagle, he described how fossils in different regions were more consistent with each other and the still living life in those regions, rather than other regions. If creatures had all been created rather than evolved, why would you see this pattern of regional similarity? The next two chapters were some of the lines of evidence that impressed me the most – Geographical Distribution. This built upon the idea touched on in the last chapter, of the similarity of organisms in certain regions compared to different regions, even when two regions may have broadly similar habitats. To give one striking example of two similar habitats that were even extremely close to one another yet geographically isolated, "No two marine faunas are more distinct, with hardly a fish, shell, or crab in common, than those of the eastern and western shores of South and Central America; yet these great faunas are separated only by the narrow, but impassable, isthmus of Panama." Some of my favorite bits of evidence from this chapter come from experiments Darwin did himself to try to better understand the ways in which seeds could be dispersed to spread the range of particular species. In one experiment, he immersed several types of seeds in salt water, periodically pulling some out and planting them, to see how long the seeds could survive such conditions (up to months in a few cases). In another, and getting his hands a bit dirtier, "In the course of two months, I picked up in my garden 12 kinds of seeds, out of the excrement of small birds, and these seemed perfect, and some of them, which I tried, germinated." In those chapters on geographical distribution, I was especially struck by his observations and data of the life on oceanic islands. Islands (or at least some of them) are self-contained, isolated habitats. From the framework of special creation and the immutability of species, the types of life on them could be anything the creator desired, and you might suspect a sort of specialized island ecosystem that was the same from island to island no matter where on Earth. But the reality is that life on islands is most similar to life on the nearest mainland, without actually being the same species. Moreover, the kinds of life on islands isn't just a representative subset of mainland life, but is biased by certain other considerations. For example, Darwin specifically noted that no mammals were ever found to be indigenous to islands more than 300 miles away from a continent, while they were indigenous on islands closer to continents. Darwin's key insight in all this was that these patterns are explained by life arriving at islands from the mainland, and then evolving to adapt to their new island life once there. The bias is explained by the types of animals that can survive the journeys. That puts birds and flying insects as very likely island inhabitants (for example, getting caught by the winds of a storm), while cold blooded animals with low food needs could survive long 'rafting events' on vegetation mats or floating debris, while mammals with their high food needs could only survive short journeys. The chapter on Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings looked at the well known similarities in the anatomy of various organisms, and how those similarities naturally form into nested hierarchies. He went into details such as homologous organs, vestigial features, embryology, etc. I haven't quoted much from Darwin throughout this answer, so here's a bit of a longer excerpt where he gets a bit more excited than normal (he used an exclamation mark): How inexplicable are these facts on the ordinary view of creation! Why should the brain be enclosed in a box composed of such numerous and such extraordinarily shaped pieces of bone? As Owen has remarked, the benefit derived from the yielding of the separate pieces in the act of parturition of mammals, will by no means explain the same construction in the skulls of birds. Why should similar bones have been created in the formation of the wing and leg of a bat, used as they are for such totally different purposes? Why should one crustacean, which has an extremely complex mouth formed of many parts, consequently always have fewer legs; or conversely, those with many legs have simpler mouths? Why should the sepals, petals, stamens, and pistils in any individual flower, though fitted for such widely different purposes, be all constructed on the same pattern? Of course, the explanation as put forth by Darwin is common ancestry, and modifying the anatomy of ancestors, rather than a creator creating organisms from scratch without constraint. The last chapter was just a summary (recapitulation) of the book as a whole, so not much for me to add in this answer as it pertains to evidence. So, that's a summary of the evidence for evolution and natural selection as according to Charles Darwin. The way we so often think of evolution as a study of the past, when I first read On the Origin of Species, I really was struck by how much Darwin relied on evidence from the present day and living organisms, and how he was able to infer common descent from the patterns in existing life. And even that was enough to convince most naturalists of his day of the truth of evolution. I think Darwin himself would be amazed to see just how many fossils people have found since then, and how many details later scientists were able to fill in.

What hasn't natural selection eliminated criminals and selfishness? Do we need a few more billion years? While evolution is a mindless process without any conscious intent, sometimes anthropomorphizing can help to explain things. And in that sense, the 'goal' of evolution is to produce more offspring. And in a social animal like us, that sets up conflicting imperatives. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups and cooperation can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. If you've ever tried working on DIY projects by yourself, you've probably found times where two people working together can get the job done in less than half the time of one person working alone. So, for example, if I help my neighbor build a shed, and then he helps me build mine, we'll get two sheds built in less time than it would have taken either of us to try to build our own. It's a win-win. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If I was the cantakerous neighbor that nobody liked, I'd never get anybody to help me on projects. But, there are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest they sacrifice their own reproductive success. I don't want to go around only helping out neighbors, but never get around to my own projects. Similarly, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole, and conversely, individuals will have an interest in not being identified as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining long term acceptance within the group. I'll give up my own time to help my neighbor move with no expectation of reward other than the obligatory pizza and beer, but it cements my standing in the community as a 'good guy'. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior, but, anthropomorphizing a bit more, natural selection was. And so, we've evolved all these instincts for noble and selfish impulses. As long as our species survives and we continue to live in these types of social groups, selfishness will unfortunately persist alongside our more noble impulses. It's the way natural selection ensures that we take care of propagating our own genes. If a ball is spinning and generating artificial gravity, would the force be on the outer surface or inner surface? A ball is not really a great shape for this. When engineers talk about spinning a spaceship or space station to create artificial gravity, what it really is is centrifugal force. I'm not going to get into a big discussion on centripetal vs. centrifugal force. Just realize that in a rotating reference frame, centrifugal force is a 'useful fiction' to help engineers calculate forces while keeping their coordinate system aligned with the rotating object, and that centripetal force points towards the axis of rotation. ABOVE: Centripetal force is the 'real' force in a non-rotating reference frame. Centrifugal force is the useful fiction from the rock's point of view. SOURCE: Centrifugal Force- Definition, Principle, Examples (vs Centripetal force) For this reason, when engineers propose rotating space ships or space stations to create 'artificial gravity', they tend to follow a few standard forms that make the best use of centrifugal force. The simplest is putting your main crew compartment and some type of counterweight on opposite ends of a tether, and having them spin around their common center of gravity, with the tether holding them together. ABOVE SOURCE: Should we give up on artificial gravity? A common one in sci-fi stories for a bigger ship/station is to make it into a ring, so that you can take advantage of the entire ring for artificial gravity. Here's the classic example from 2001: A Space Odyssey: SOURCE: Sci-fi Gifs And here's kind of what it would be like inside such a station: SOURCE: Quora For the really fanciful sci-fi stories, they might use something know as an O'Neill cylinder. This is a truly gigantic version, where you have a huge cylinder spinning, which can create entire enclosed habitats: ABOVE: I know the labels are in Russian (I can't read them, either), but it's about the best diagram I could find SOURCE: Humanoid History (@HumanoidHistory) on X That said, there are some very significant engineering challenges to doing any of these configurations, such that none of them may be practical, especially in the near term. For any upcoming missions to Mars, for example, the astronauts are probably just going to have to deal with a zero-g journey. So, with all that explanation, I hope the answer to your question is obvious. The artificial gravity will be on the inside surface of your spinning ball, due to the centrifugal force 'pushing' you away from the axis of rotation. If you were on the outside surface, you would be flung away from the ship/station. But you should also see why a ball wouldn't be a great shape for this. Only the 'equator' would have the centrifugal force perpendicular to its surface. Everywhere else would be on a slope, like a hill. The points right at the axis of rotation would be completely vertical from an astronaut's perspective.
